meta.title: GitHub Workflow MCP
meta.description: A Model Context Protocol server that gives AI agents structured, scoped access to your GitHub engineering workflow.

tools.name: list_repositories
tools.summary: Show all repositories the agent has access to in your organisation.
tools.description: List all repositories in the configured GitHub organisation. Returns name, description, default branch, and visibility for each repo. Results are cached.

tools.name: get_repository
tools.summary: Get detailed information about a specific repository.
tools.description: Fetch metadata for a single repository — language, topics, open issue count, size, and visibility.

tools.name: get_file
tools.summary: Read the contents of a file from a repository.
tools.description: Fetch a file's content from a repository at a given ref. Paths with wildcards, double-dots, or absolute roots are rejected. Content is base64-decoded automatically.

inputs.name: path
inputs.description: File path within the repository (e.g. src/index.ts).

inputs.name: ref
inputs.description: Git ref (branch, tag, or SHA). Defaults to the default branch.

tools.name: search_code
tools.summary: Search for code patterns or symbols across a repository.
tools.description: Search for code within a single repository using GitHub code search. Returns file path, URL, and a matched snippet. Query must not contain GitHub qualifier syntax (e.g. repo:, org:).

inputs.name: query
inputs.description: Search terms. Must not contain GitHub qualifier syntax.

tools.name: get_active_work
tools.summary: See all open pull requests and issues currently assigned to the agent.
tools.description: Return open pull requests and issues assigned to the authenticated GitHub user across all allowed repositories. Useful as a starting point for understanding what work is in progress.

returns.description: Separated lists of pull requests and issues.

tools.name: get_issue
tools.summary: Get the full details of a single issue.
tools.description: Fetch title, body, labels, assignees, and state for a single issue. Does not include comment history.

tools.name: search_issues
tools.summary: Search for issues in a repository by keyword.
tools.description: Search issues using GitHub query syntax. Returns up to 20 results per page. Query must not contain GitHub qualifier syntax.

tools.name: list_pull_requests
tools.summary: List pull requests in a repository.
tools.description: List pull requests in a repository. Returns number, title, state, draft flag, head/base branch, author, and URL. Defaults to open PRs. Use before get_pr to find the PR number.

inputs.name: state
inputs.description: Filter by PR state. Defaults to open.

tools.name: get_pr
tools.summary: Get the details of a pull request.
tools.description: Fetch title, body, state, head/base branch, author, requested reviewers, labels, and merge status for a pull request. Does not include commit history or file contents.

tools.name: get_changed_files
tools.summary: List which files were changed in a pull request.
tools.description: Returns files changed in a PR with their status (added/modified/deleted), line counts, and patch hunks. Does not return full file contents.

tools.name: get_release_status
tools.summary: Check the latest release of a repository.
tools.description: Fetch the latest GitHub release — tag name, publish date, draft/prerelease status, and a summary of the release notes (capped at 500 characters).

tools.name: get_recent_deployments
tools.summary: See the last 10 CI/CD workflow runs for a repository.
tools.description: Fetch the 10 most recent GitHub Actions workflow runs — name, status, conclusion, trigger event, branch, and timestamps.

tools.name: get_workflow_run
tools.summary: Get full detail for a specific workflow run by ID.
tools.description: Fetch status, conclusion, branch, commit SHA, trigger actor, and URL for a single GitHub Actions workflow run. Use when you have a run ID from get_recent_deployments and need to inspect it more closely.

tools.name: get_workflow_run_jobs
tools.summary: List all jobs in a workflow run with per-step conclusions.
tools.description: Fetch every job in a workflow run, including per-step name, status, and conclusion. Use to pinpoint exactly which step inside which job failed.

returns.description: Array of jobs with step detail.

tools.name: get_failed_job_logs
tools.summary: Fetch the raw log output for a failed workflow job.
tools.description: Download the log output for a specific job (identified by job_id from get_workflow_run_jobs). Returns the tail of the log, capped at 50 KB, so the failure message is always included. Use to read the actual error without opening the browser.

output.logs:
##[error]Process completed with exit code 1.
  ● Test suite failed to run
    Cannot find module...

tools.name: rerun_failed_jobs
tools.summary: Trigger a rerun of only the failed jobs in a workflow run.
tools.description: Requeue the failed jobs in a workflow run without rerunning jobs that already passed. Use after diagnosing a transient CI failure. Requires ALLOW_WRITES=true.

inputs.name: run_id
inputs.description: Workflow run ID whose failed jobs to rerun.

returns.description: Confirmation that the rerun was queued.

tools.name: lint_code
tools.summary: Check a piece of code for errors and style issues.
tools.description: Lint a string of code inline. The filename is used to infer the language and resolve linter config. ESLint and TypeScript config are loaded from LINT_CWD (defaults to the server's own directory — set LINT_CWD to your project root to enforce your team's rules). Returns violations with severity, rule ID, line/column, explanation, and suggested fix. Input is capped at 100 KB.

inputs.name: filename
inputs.description: Filename (e.g. src/utils.ts). Used to select the linter and resolve config — the file does not need to exist on disk.

tools.name: validate_diff
tools.summary: Lint the changed lines in a git diff.
tools.description: Lint a unified diff string (e.g. from git diff). Each added/changed hunk is linted in context using the config from LINT_CWD. Returns violations mapped to their new-file line numbers. Input is capped at 100 KB.

inputs.name: diff
inputs.description: Unified diff string (output of git diff or similar).

returns.description: Array of violations with filename attached.

tools.name: validate_pr
tools.summary: Lint all changed files in a pull request.
tools.description: Fetch a pull request's changed files from GitHub and lint the modified content. Returns violations grouped by filename. Respects the ALLOWED_REPOS allowlist. Use to check a PR for lint errors before reviewing or merging.

returns.description: Array of violations across all changed files.

output.explanation: Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number'

tools.name: suggest_fixes
tools.summary: Turn lint violations into actionable edit suggestions.
tools.description: Convert lint violations into structured edit suggestions. Returns only violations that have a suggested fix. Never writes to disk — the agent decides what to do with the suggestions.

inputs.name: violations
inputs.description: Violations from lint_code, validate_diff, or validate_pr.

tools.name: apply_safe_fixes
tools.summary: Automatically fix safe lint issues and commit them to a branch.
tools.description: Apply ESLint autofixable rules (formatting, import ordering, whitespace) to source code and commit the result to a branch. Returns a unified diff of the changes. Never touches logic, types, or renames. Requires ALLOW_WRITES=true. To write to an existing branch set only branch. To create a new branch first, set both branch (new name) and base_branch (source).

inputs.name: branch
inputs.description: Branch to commit fixes to. If this branch does not yet exist, supply base_branch to create it.

inputs.name: base_branch
inputs.description: If provided, creates branch from this base before committing. Omit to write to an already-existing branch.

returns.description: Branch name and unified diff of applied changes, or a message if no fixes were needed.

tools.name: search_knowledge
tools.summary: Search your team's engineering knowledge base.
tools.description: Search the engineering knowledge base for process docs, architecture notes, and coding guidelines using trigram similarity. Use before asking about team conventions, on-call runbooks, or project standards. Returns ranked excerpts with source file and section heading. Requires DATABASE_URL to be set.

results.excerpt: Use camelCase for variables and functions...

tools.name: create_or_update_file
tools.summary: Write or update a single file on an existing branch.
tools.description: Write or update a single file in a repository on an existing branch. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites it if it does. Use create_branch first if the branch doesn't exist. Requires ALLOW_WRITES=true. All write operations are audit-logged when a database is connected.

inputs.name: path
inputs.description: File path within the repository (e.g. src/router.ts).

inputs.name: branch
inputs.description: Branch to commit to (must already exist).

tools.name: create_branch
tools.summary: Create a new branch in a repository.
tools.description: Create a new branch from a base ref. Resolves the base SHA automatically. Branch name is validated against a safe character allowlist before the request is sent. Use this as the first step before writing files or opening a pull request. Requires ALLOW_WRITES=true.

inputs.name: base
inputs.description: Branch, tag, or SHA to branch from.

tools.name: create_pull_request
tools.summary: Open a pull request.
tools.description: Open a pull request between two branches. Use after pushing commits to a branch created with create_branch. Requires ALLOW_WRITES=true. All write operations are audit-logged when a database is connected.

tools.name: request_review
tools.summary: Ask specific people to review a pull request.
tools.description: Add reviewer(s) to an open pull request. Use after create_pull_request when the PR is ready for human review. Requires ALLOW_WRITES=true.

inputs.name: reviewers
inputs.description: GitHub usernames to request review from.

tools.name: merge_pr
tools.summary: Merge a pull request.
tools.description: Merge a pull request. Only call when the PR is approved and CI checks have passed. Defaults to squash merge. Requires ALLOW_WRITES=true.

content.body: GitHub Workflow MCP is a Model Context Protocol server that exposes your GitHub engineering workflow to AI agents. It gives agents structured, scoped access to repositories, pull requests, issues, CI runs, linting tooling, and an engineering knowledge base — enough to understand and participate in the software delivery lifecycle.

The server is designed as a company scaffold: the tool definitions, transport layer, and knowledge structure are all in place, but the knowledge content is intentionally left empty so your team can fill it in without touching any code.
All write operations are disabled by default. Set ALLOW_WRITES=true to enable them. Every write is audit-logged when a database is connected.

items: Expose workflows, not raw systems — tools map to tasks, not API endpoints
Prefer retrieval over preloading — agents fetch what they need, when they need it
Tools are small, composable, and deterministic
Least-privilege access — reads are always safe, writes require explicit opt-in
Multi-repository from day one — all tools accept a repo parameter and respect ALLOWED_REPOS

content.body: Prerequisites: Node.js ≥ 20, a GitHub fine-grained PAT with repo read scope.

git clone https://github.com/Wajkie/github-workflow-mcp
cd github-workflow-mcp
npm install
cp .env.example .env
# Edit .env — set GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_ORG at minimum
npm run dev
The server starts on stdio by default. Set PORT to also enable the HTTP transport.
Build the project first, then add the server to your Claude Desktop config.
npm run build

content.label: claude_desktop_config.json

vars.name: GITHUB_TOKEN
vars.description: Fine-grained PAT. Needs repo read scope; add write scope if ALLOW_WRITES=true.

vars.name: ALLOWED_REPOS
vars.description: Comma-separated list of repository names the agent may access. Use * for all repos.

vars.name: ALLOW_WRITES
vars.description: Set to true to enable write tools (create_branch, create_pull_request, request_review, merge_pr, apply_safe_fixes, rerun_failed_jobs).

vars.name: LINT_CWD
vars.description: Absolute path to the project directory whose eslint.config.js and tsconfig.json should be used for linting. Point this at your project root so lint_code, validate_diff, validate_pr, and apply_safe_fixes enforce your team's actual rules.

vars.name: PORT
vars.description: Enables the HTTP transport when set. Both stdio and HTTP run simultaneously when PORT is present.

vars.name: MCP_SECRET
vars.description: If set, all /mcp requests must include an x-mcp-secret header matching this value.

vars.name: MAX_BODY_BYTES
vars.description: Maximum HTTP request body size in bytes.

vars.name: MAX_SESSIONS
vars.description: Maximum number of concurrent HTTP MCP sessions.

vars.name: DATABASE_URL
vars.description: Postgres connection string. Enables audit logging and knowledge search.

vars.name: REDIS_URL
vars.description: Redis connection string. Enables response caching.

vars.name: CACHE_TTL_REPOS
vars.description: Repository list cache TTL in seconds.

vars.name: CACHE_TTL_PRS
vars.description: Pull request cache TTL in seconds.

vars.name: CACHE_TTL_FILES
vars.description: File content cache TTL in seconds.

vars.name: METRICS_INTERVAL
vars.description: Emit a metrics summary log entry every N tool calls.

content.body: The server is split into three layers: transport, tool registration, and domain logic. Transport (stdio and HTTP) is wired in server.ts. Tool registration files (*Tools.ts) bind Zod-validated MCP schemas to domain functions. Domain files contain pure GitHub API calls with no MCP dependency.
The observability middleware monkey-patches McpServer.registerTool at startup, wrapping every handler with latency tracking and structured logging — no changes to individual tool handlers are needed.

Two transports run simultaneously when PORT is set. stdio uses a single shared McpServer instance. HTTP creates a separate McpServer per session (via StreamableHTTPServerTransport) so session state is isolated. Both share the same Octokit instance, audit logger, cache, and observability middleware.

When PORT is set, two additional HTTP endpoints are available. GET /health returns { "status": "ok", "linters": [...] } — the linters array lists which linting engines were detected at startup (e.g. ["eslint", "typescript"]). An empty array means no ESLint config was found; a warning is also emitted in the startup log in that case. GET /audit serves the audit log dashboard.

The knowledge/ directory contains Markdown files registered as MCP resources at engineering:///<slug>. On startup, the server reads the directory and registers one resource per file — no config required to add new files. When DATABASE_URL is set, files are also chunked by heading and indexed in Postgres using pg_trgm for full-text search via the search_knowledge tool.

All user-controlled text returned by the server passes through a shared sanitizer (src/sanitize.ts) before reaching the agent. This covers knowledge base reads and search excerpts, and GitHub API responses — issue bodies, PR bodies, and release notes. Lines matching known prompt-injection signatures are redacted: instruction overrides ("ignore all previous instructions"), role delimiter tags (<system>, [INST], <|im_start|>), persona hijacking ("act as an unrestricted..."), and explicit override commands.

railway login
railway init
railway up

Add a Postgres plugin in the Railway dashboard to enable audit logging and knowledge search. DATABASE_URL is injected automatically. Set GITHUB_TOKEN, GITHUB_ORG, and MCP_SECRET in Settings → Variables.

cp .env.example .env
# Fill in GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_ORG
docker compose up --build
Starts the MCP server on port 3000 and a Postgres 16 instance. The MCP service waits for Postgres to be healthy before starting.

This is a connector that lets AI assistants (like Claude) understand and interact with your team's software development work on GitHub. Without it, an AI assistant has no idea what your team is working on, what code looks like, or what your processes are. With it, you can ask an AI to help review a pull request, explain what an issue is about, or check whether a piece of code follows your team's standards.
Think of it as giving your AI assistant a read-only window into your engineering workflow — with the option to let it take actions too, when your team is ready.
The AI can only see repositories and take actions that your team explicitly allows. Everything is configurable, and write actions (like creating a pull request) are turned off by default.
By default the assistant can read but not change anything. Here is what it can look at:

items.label: Repositories
items.summary: See all the code projects your team has on GitHub — names, descriptions, and languages used.

items.label: Files
items.summary: Read the contents of any file in any allowed repository, at any point in its history.

items.label: Pull requests
items.summary: See who opened a PR, what it changes, who has been asked to review it, and whether it is ready to merge.

items.label: Issues
items.summary: Read the description and status of any issue, or search across issues by keyword.

items.label: Releases and deployments
items.summary: Check what version of a project was last released and whether recent CI builds passed or failed.

items.label: CI failure diagnostics
items.summary: Drill into a failed CI run to see which job and step failed, and read the raw log output — without opening the browser.

items.label: Your in-progress work
items.summary: Ask the assistant to summarise everything currently assigned to you across all repositories.

items.label: Team knowledge base
items.summary: Search your team's own engineering guidelines, conventions, and architecture notes.

content.body: Write actions are turned off by default. A team administrator must explicitly enable them by setting ALLOW_WRITES=true. Every action is logged.

content.body: A team member opens a pull request. Before a human reviewer looks at it, an AI assistant can automatically check the changed code against the team's style rules, flag any obvious issues, and summarise what changed in plain language. The reviewer arrives with context already prepared.

items: Assistant fetches the changed files from the PR
Runs them through the project's linting rules
Posts a summary comment (if write tools are enabled)

pages.title: Getting a new engineer up to speed

content.body: A new engineer joins the team. Instead of reading through dozens of wiki pages, they can ask the AI assistant questions directly. The assistant searches the knowledge base and reads relevant files on their behalf, answering questions about conventions, architecture decisions, and where to find things.

When write tools are enabled, an AI assistant can take a GitHub issue, understand the requirement, find relevant code in the repository, generate a fix, lint it, and open a pull request for human review — all in one conversation.

items: Read the issue to understand what needs to change
Search the codebase to find the relevant files
Read the team's conventions from the knowledge base
Lint it to confirm it meets standards
Create a branch and open a pull request for human review

content.body: During an incident or before a release, quickly ask the AI assistant: 'What version of the API is currently live?', 'Did the last CI run pass?', or 'What changed since the last release?' — without leaving the conversation.
The assistant only has access to repositories your team explicitly allows. By default it can see all repositories in your GitHub organisation, but this can be restricted to a specific list.

Write actions — creating branches, opening pull requests, merging — are turned off by default. They require an administrator to opt in, and every action taken is recorded in an audit log that shows who triggered it, what was done, and when.
The assistant never has access to your GitHub password or SSH keys — it uses a limited-scope access token that can be revoked at any time.
Your GitHub token and any secrets are never returned in tool responses. They stay on the server and are never visible to the AI or in conversation history.

Any text that comes from GitHub — issue descriptions, pull request bodies, release notes — as well as the knowledge base files, is automatically scanned before it reaches the AI. If those sources contain hidden instructions designed to manipulate the AI's behaviour, those lines are removed before the content is served.
